pointers.sentence: Each refusal has a **reason**, a short sentence that is logged and handed to the failure view (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._reject`).

`CsrfViewMiddleware._accept` marks an accepted request with the attribute `"csrf_processing_done"`, and `process_view` returns at once for a request so marked (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._accept`).

It is tested after `CsrfViewMiddleware.process_request` has read the browser's secret, so `get_token` in an exempt view still uses that secret (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`).

Last, the test client's flag: its handler sets `"_dont_enforce_csrf_checks"` on every request, true unless the client was made with `enforce_csrf_checks=True` ([The test client: `Client` and `ClientHandler`](../testing/client.md)) (`django/test/client.py:ClientHandler.__call__`).

A request with an `"Origin"` header is refused unless `CsrfViewMiddleware._origin_verified` accepts it, in one of three ways tried in order (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._origin_verified`).

Or it may have the scheme of a trusted origin written with a `"*"`, and a host that matches that origin's host, star taken off, by `is_same_domain`, where a pattern that begins with a dot matches the domain and every subdomain (`django/utils/http.py:is_same_domain`).

The same host over HTTP is compared with no trusted host, since no trusted origin has that scheme: the one `is_same_domain` under it is `get_host`'s, which tests the `"Host"` against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (`django/http/request.py:validate_host`).

The setting is read by each instance of the middleware, as the first request alone shows: `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` goes into three cached properties, each the first time the instance needs it and never again (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.allowed_origin_subdomains`).

A system check made for the change, `check_csrf_trusted_origins`, still reports a value without `"://"` as `"4_0.E001"` (`docs/releases/1.9.txt`, `docs/releases/4.0.txt`, `django/core/checks/compatibility/django_4_0.py:check_csrf_trusted_origins`).

A system check made for the change, `check_csrf_trusted_origins`, still reports a value without `"://"` as `"4_0.E001"` (`docs/releases/1.9.txt`, `docs/releases/4.0.txt`, `django/core/checks/compatibility/django_4_0.py:check_csrf_trusted_origins`).

A system check made for the change, `check_csrf_trusted_origins`, still reports a value without `"://"` as `"4_0.E001"` (`docs/releases/1.9.txt`, `docs/releases/4.0.txt`, `django/core/checks/compatibility/django_4_0.py:check_csrf_trusted_origins`).

Only a request with no `"Origin"` has its `"Referer"` read, and only if it is secure; over plain HTTP such a request goes on to the token with neither header read (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`).

The cookie is what makes this work: browsers accept a cookie set over plain HTTP even for a site they reach over HTTPS, and since a secret kept in the cookie is tied to no session, a secret of the attacker's making serves as well as the site's (`docs/ref/csrf.txt`).

The check can afford to be that strict because the `"Referer"` is seldom missing over HTTPS: Barth et al. found it absent from same-domain HTTPS requests in about 0.2% of cases or fewer (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`).

When the domain is `None`, as by default, the host must match `get_host`, which includes any port, and a `DisallowedHost` from `get_host` is refused with `REASON_BAD_REFERER` (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._check_referer`).

A request with no secret is refused too, and **login CSRF** is among the attacks that stops: another site tricking a user's browser into logging into this one with someone else's credentials (`docs/ref/csrf.txt`) (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._check_token`).

A request with no secret is refused too, and **login CSRF** is among the attacks that stops: another site tricking a user's browser into logging into this one with someone else's credentials (`docs/ref/csrf.txt`) (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._check_token`).
No other body is read, so a `"PUT"` with a good token only in its form-encoded body is refused with `"CSRF token missing."` (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._check_token`).
The token must then be 32 or 64 letters and digits (`django/middleware/csrf.py:_check_token_format`).

`_does_token_match` unmasks a token of 64, takes one of 32 as the secret itself, as a script that read the cookie sends it, and compares it with the secret by `constant_time_compare` ([Secret keys and `django.utils.crypto`](keys.md)) (`django/middleware/csrf.py:_does_token_match`).

The reason for a malformed or wrong token names where the token was found, the form or the header, as in `"CSRF token from the 'X-Csrftoken' HTTP header has incorrect length."` (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._bad_token_message`).

`CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view` makes the origin test's reason in place; the `"Referer"` and token tests raise `RejectRequest` with theirs, which `process_view` catches; and each refusal ends in `CsrfViewMiddleware._reject`, given the reason (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware.process_view`).

`CsrfViewMiddleware._reject` calls the view `CSRF_FAILURE_VIEW` names, imported by `get_callable`, with the request and the reason, and logs the response it gets back by `log_response` on the logger `"django.security.csrf"`, as `"Forbidden (%s): %s"` with the reason and the path; that response goes out through the chain in the view's place (`django/middleware/csrf.py:CsrfViewMiddleware._reject`).
The security checks import the view and test that it takes a request and a reason ([The security checks](checks.md)) (`django/core/checks/security/csrf.py:check_csrf_failure_view`).

`_reject` is a method so that a subclass can replace it: the class of `requires_csrf_token`, like that of `ensure_csrf_cookie`, replaces it with one that refuses nothing ([A middleware as a decorator](../views/middleware-decorators.md)) (`django/views/decorators/csrf.py`).

`log_response` logs a 4xx as a warning and marks the response as logged, so that the handler, which logs a response of 400 or more to `"django.request"`, does not log it again ([Logging](../startup/logging.md#log_response-a-response-is-logged-once)) (`django/utils/log.py:log_response`).

`csrf_failure` asks the project's template engines for `"403_csrf.html"`, and when none has it renders the built-in `"csrf_403.html"`, with an `Engine` of its own, which does not read `TEMPLATES`; either page goes back in an `HttpResponseForbidden` (`django/views/csrf.py:csrf_failure`).
The built-in page's context holds the reason and two flags, `"no_referer"` and `"no_cookie"`, true under `REASON_NO_REFERER` and `REASON_NO_CSRF_COOKIE` (`django/views/csrf.py:csrf_failure`).

The page shows its paragraphs for a missing `"Referer"` or cookie only under those two reasons, and the reason itself, with a list of what to check, only when `settings.DEBUG` is true (`django/views/templates/csrf_403.html`).

`csrf_failure` renders it with the request alone, so it sees what a `RequestContext` gives it, the context processors' values, and nothing of the view's: a template that writes `{{ reason }}`, `{{ no_cookie }}` and `{{ csp_nonce }}` renders the first two empty and the third, where the engine has the `csp` processor, with the nonce (`django/views/csrf.py:csrf_failure`).
